notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from the older commentators (Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Clarke, Keil & Delitzsch), from Precept Austin, Enduring Word (David Guzik) and Bible.org (Utley). I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and no page by a named prosperity or word-of-faith teacher. So those sections are left out or kept thin. The sources do not split cleanly along denominational lines. The main disagreement is over how far the promises still apply (see the end).

**Background to the chapter**
- Bible Hub's summary says the blessing-and-curse pattern copies ancient Near Eastern treaties, with God as the overlord. Blessing-and-curse language mirrors ancient Near-Eastern treaties: vassal loyalty brought prosperity; rebellion triggered the suzerain's judgment. Here the suzerain is the LORD Himself. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28.htm
- Guzik: God meant to show Himself to the world through Israel. Either they would be so blessed that only God could explain it, or so cursed that only God could explain their survival. God was determined to reveal Himself to the world through Israel. Yahweh would do this either by making them so blessed that the world would know only God could have blessed them so; or by making them so cursed that only God could have cursed them and cause them to still survive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/
- Matthew Henry reads the chapter as more than conditional terms. He sees it as a prediction that Israel would prosper for a while and later be ruined by disobedience. These are both there and here delivered, not only as sanctions of the law, what should be conditionally, but as predictions of the event, what would be certainly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/28.htm

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary says obedience was the essential condition for enjoying any of God's gifts. The condition sine qua non of all enjoyment of the Divine bounty was obedience on the part of the people to the word and Law of Jehovah their God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-28.html
- Precept Austin points out the repeated "if" (vv. 1, 2, 9, 13, 15, 58). It says these terms belong to the Sinai covenant and should be kept separate from the unconditional covenant with Abraham. Note the conditional nature of the blessing is emphasized by the repetitive use of IF - Dt 28:1, 2, 9, 13. It also notes there is no "Amen" after these blessings, unlike the twelve curses in ch. 27. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary

**v. 2**
- Henry: some good people feel unworthy and back away from blessing, but the blessing will find them anyway. Good people sometimes, under the sense of their unworthiness, are ready to fly from the blessing and to conclude that it belongs not to them,; but the blessing shall find them out and follow them notwithstanding. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/28.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary (J. Orr, citing Keil) says blessing and curse are pictured as real powers that chase the nation. Blessing and curse, as Keil says, are viewed in these verses "as actual powers, which follow in the footsteps of the nation, and overtake it". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-28.html

**vv. 3–6 (city and country, womb, basket, coming and going)**
- The Pulpit Commentary: The fullness of the blessing in all the relations of life, external and internal, is presented in six particulars, each introduced by the word "blessed." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/28.htm
- v. 3: Henry says the blessing reaches people wherever they live and whatever their work, in town or country. Whether their habitation was in town or country, whether they were husbandmen or tradesmen, whether their business called them into the city or into the field, they should be preserved https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-7.html
- v. 4: A Bible Hub article links the three areas (womb, soil, livestock) to "be fruitful" in Genesis 1:28, as an echo of Eden's abundance. The verse's threefold fertility formula—womb, soil, livestock—mirrors the triad in Genesis 1:28 https://biblehub.com/q/Deut_28_4_s_link_to_blessings_curses.htm
- v. 5: The Pulpit Commentary says the basket stands for stored produce and the kneading-trough for daily use of it. "the basket" representing the store in which the fruits of the earth were laid up, the "kneading-trough" the use of these for the supply of daily needs https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-28.html. Precept Austin: Moses is saying they would never starve, never lack for adequate supply of food and nourishment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary
- v. 6: Guzik, quoting Thompson, says "come in… go out" is a common Old Testament way of describing all of a person's affairs. The point is God's favour over the whole of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/ Ellicott adds a possible deeper meaning. These words may apply to the details of life, or they may have a further meaning, as the eisodus of Christ was His entrance into this world's labour, and His exodus His departure https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm

**v. 7**
- Gill: The phrase is expressive of an entire victory, and of a complete rout and dispersion of an enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-7.html
- Ellicott quotes Rashi: "So is the custom of them that are terrified, to flee, scattering in every direction". He points to the flight of the Midianites (Judges 7) and the Syrians (2 Kings 7). https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-7.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary (R.M. Edgar) says seven, the perfect number, means a perfect defeat. The promise is about defending the land, not about conquest abroad. The Lord will not encourage them in a "spirited foreign policy," but will make them invincible defenders of their hearths and homes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-28.html
- Currid, quoted by Precept Austin, says Israel had already seen this at the Exodus and in the wilderness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary

**v. 8**
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says the promise covers all their work. It adds a warning: If rich, we must not be idle. Accumulation of wealth may be accumulation of sorrow. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/deuteronomy-28.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik counts this as perhaps the best blessing, because without God's presence the material blessings would be empty. He quotes Clarke: "This is the sum of all blessings, to be made holy, and be preserved in holiness." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/
- Henry says obedience has to last. Not only do them for once, but keep them for ever; not only set out in his ways, but walk in them to the end. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-7.html

**v. 10**
- Utley (via Precept Austin) says God meant to bless Israel to catch the nations' attention and draw them to Himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary
- Guzik gives the queen of Sheba visiting Solomon (1 Kings 10) as an example of a nation seeing God's hand on Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

**v. 11**
- Precept Austin says this almost repeats v. 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62510/ Bible Hub notes that the Hebrew word for "prosper" carries the idea of surplus. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik quotes Kalland: the Canaanites believed Baal controlled the rain, but Moses insisted it was the LORD who would send it or hold it back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

**v. 13**
- Keil & Delitzsch say "head, not tail" is a picture taken from everyday life, explained by the next phrase. thou wilt rise more and more, and increase in wealth, power, and dignity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-14.htm

**v. 14**
- Gill says turning aside to other gods would break the first table of the law (the commandments about God), than which nothing was more abominable and provoking to God. Another commentary on the same page says Moses ends the blessings by restating the condition he started with. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik reminds readers that Israel agreed to these curses as part of the covenant, at Sinai (Exodus 24) and again here. He quotes Trapp on why there are more curses than blessings: "Such is the baseness of our natures, that we are sooner terrified with menaces than moved with mercies." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/
- Henry says the curse is never without cause. Its root is ignoring God's voice, which he calls the highest contempt possible. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_028.cfm
- Ellicott thinks the curse section may be longer because Israel's disasters under the Sinai covenant would last more years than its prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html. Jack Deere (via Precept Austin) says the longer curse section was meant to foreshadow Israel's eventual failure. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary

**vv. 16–19**
- The Pulpit Commentary: As the blessing was set forth in six announcements (Deuteronomy 28:3-6), the curse is proclaimed in form and number corresponding (Deuteronomy 28:16-19). The curse thus appears as the exact counterpart of the blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-28.html
- v. 17: Precept Austin says the empty basket and bowl mean famine and starvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary
- v. 18: Precept Austin says barren wombs would replace many healthy children. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62510/
- v. 19: Precept Austin says "coming in" means home and family life, "going out" means business life; together, every area of life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62510/

**v. 20**
- Ellicott notes that each of the three nouns has "the" in Hebrew, just as if they were so many diseases. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-20.htm
- Henry applies the frustration in all one's work to anyone whose heart is set on the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/28.htm
- John MacArthur (gty.org) quotes vv. 20–22 to describe the "curse of the law" that Christ redeems believers from in Galatians 3:13. https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-285/redeemed-from-the-curse-of-the-law

**vv. 21–22**
- Henry separates two cases. God sometimes uses sickness to discipline His own people; here disease is a sign of wrath. according to the temper of our spirits, under sickness, accordingly it is to us a blessing or a curse. But, whatever sickness may be to particular persons, it is certain that epidemical diseases raging among a people are national judgments https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_028.cfm
- Ellicott quotes Rashi on the fever, "A disease which heats the body inwardly". He links blight and mildew to Amos 4:9 and Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 8:37. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm
- Barnes says "blasting" is the damage from the scorching east wind and "mildew" is a blight on the green ear of grain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-23.htm
- Utley notes the word for mildew means "green." He counts seven afflictions, matching seven blessings in the chapter. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28

**v. 23**
- Gill: the sky is like bronze because it is dry and hard, not because it shines; the ground is like iron, too hard to plough. He notes that Leviticus 26:19 reverses the two metals but means the same thing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-28.html
- Calvin draws a lesson about God's care. not even a drop of rain falls to the earth except distilled by God, and that whenever it rains, the earth is irrigated as if by His hand. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-23.html
- Ellicott: the image covers more than drought. It means God's refusal to remove it. He compares Jeremiah 14, where God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm
- JFB calls these strong Oriental figures used to describe the effects of long-continued drought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_028.cfm
- Bible Hub's study notes add that the bronze sky can suggest prayers that do not get through. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-23.htm

**Where interpreters differ (not neatly by denomination)**
- **Who the promises are for.**
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the blessings were Given to Israel first, but for every nation that fears God and keeps His commands. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/deuteronomy-28.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch (via Constable) say the blessing was only partly fulfilled in the Old Testament. Its full fulfilment awaits Israel's future restoration (Romans 11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-28.html. Precept Austin agrees and expects a future restoration of the nation of Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary
  - Guzik likewise says God is not finished with Israel. He adds that the church's persecution of Jews brought a curse on the church itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/
  - Kelly makes a sharp contrast: these are earthly blessings for Israel, while the sinner needs acceptance with God, not merely to receive in his basket and in his store. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-23.html
- **The Methodist voice.** Studylight labels Adam Clarke Wesleyan/Methodist · Arminianism. He reads v. 7 as a promise of safety from invasion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-7.html. On v. 23 he reads the bronze sky as no early or latter rain, leaving ground too hard to farm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-23.html. His reading is close to Calvin's and Gill's; I found no real Methodist-versus-Reformed split on these verses.
- **Christ and the curse.** Several sources read vv. 15–23 through Galatians 3:13, where Christ bears the curse of the law: MacArthur (gty.org link above), Bible Hub https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-15.htm, and Precept Austin (link above).

**Popular modern teaching (prosperity)**
- Precept Austin warns against taking these national promises as personal guarantees. The blessings and curses came to be removed from their covenant context and were applied contractually to individuals, so that wealth was regarded as symptomatic of righteousness, and suffering as consequential of sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary
- A Bible Hub article sets the chapter beside Job. It says God is not mechanically bound to dispense prosperity or pain strictly as a response to personal moral performance. https://biblehub.com/q/why_does_deut._28_link_prosperity_to_obedience.htm
- For a contrast, Everett's Study Notes applies the verses very broadly. For example, he reads v. 8 as God blessing financial institutions, such as banking, insurance, investment planning, real estate, etc. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/deuteronomy-28.html. The page does not say which tradition he belongs to, so I haven't labelled him.
